Volume 11 · Chapter 09

Currency, sovereign and cross-border risk

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c08

By the endAnalyze international claims with explicit currency and jurisdiction assumptions.

An international claim has more than one address

Capability. Map a claim's currency, obligor, creditor residence, governing rules and payment account; derive a covered currency hedge; reconcile its dated cash needs; and separate sovereign repayment capacity from a specified willingness decision. The prerequisite is insurance, pensions and household finance. We also use external accounts and currency quotation, forward cash flows and margin, and funding ladders. No stochastic exchange-rate model, sovereign default equilibrium or present-day legal rule is assumed.

A company owns enough foreign cash to cover a domestic-currency loan after conversion. It also holds a forward that offsets exchange-rate movements. Yet its offshore lender is unpaid: the foreign cash cannot be transferred before the deadline, and the derivative is a separate contract. Meanwhile a sovereign reports substantial reserves and a modest net external position but must refinance a large gross payment tomorrow. These are questions about particular claims and particular clocks. Adding amounts after translation into one reporting currency does not establish payment capacity.

All numerical institutions, restrictions, prices, probabilities and preferences in this chapter are original synthetic assumptions. H and F are different currencies; S means H per F. A rise in S is appreciation of F against H. Amounts may be read as millions of the indicated currency, but every amount in an equation uses the same scale. Labels such as onshore and offshore refer to the stipulated account location, not a real jurisdiction. The chapter supplies no current country rating, exchange control, legal opinion or observed spread.

1. Describe the claim before measuring exposure

Write down the obligor and whether a guarantee actually reaches that obligor; the currency and index in which the amount is determined; the currency actually delivered; the payment date and intraday cutoff; the paying and receiving accounts; and any conversion, transfer, collateral or set-off right. Next identify governing law, forum, priority, amendment terms, guarantee conditions and assets available for enforcement. Those are items requiring verified contracts and jurisdiction-specific advice in an actual decision. A foreign-law label alone supplies neither an earlier receipt nor a numerical recovery rate.

Transaction exposure is sensitivity of contractual cash to exchange rates. Translation exposure changes the reporting-currency value of an unchanged balance. Economic exposure also includes how prices, demand, costs, competition and financing respond. A net F receivable is a natural offset against an F payable only to the extent their amounts, dates, entities and available accounts match. Subtracting a future subsidiary dividend from today's parent debt presupposes distribution authority and timing; consolidation in a report does not prove either.

Four independent classifications of hypothetical sovereign claims
ClaimDenominationCreditor residenceStipulated governing rulesExternal debt by residence?
A100 FResidentHome forumNo
B36 HNonresidentHome forumYes
C40 FNonresidentForeign forumYes
D80 HResidentForeign forumNo

These are classification examples, not four entries to add to the later sovereign ledger. Residence and currency answer different questions. The March 2025 pre-edited BPM 7 passages already studied in Volume 6 supply the residence-based external-account framework; this chapter does not claim that every country's published series has adopted that version. A resident can bear foreign-currency risk, and a nonresident can own local-currency debt. Nor does a net external position reveal the gross amounts that mature first.

2. What covered interest parity proves

Let RH and RF be positive gross accumulation factors to the same maturity, and let K be the forward delivery price in H/F. Assume both borrowing and lending are possible at these same factors, both currencies can be bought, sold and transferred at S₀, all counterparties perform, the forward can be signed in either direction with zero initial price, and there are no taxes, spreads, margin costs or quantity restrictions. Then:

K = S₀RH/RF.

Funded proof. Borrow S₀ H, buy 1 F and deposit it. At maturity receive RF F, sell that amount forward and repay S₀RH H. The certain H profit is KRF−S₀RH. If positive, the stated trades form an arbitrage. Conversely, borrow 1 F, sell it for S₀ H, invest the H, and buy RF F forward to repay the foreign loan. Profit is S₀RH−KRF. Prohibiting both positive profits forces equality. No probability distribution for the future spot enters either trade. Net interest may be negative: the proof requires positive gross factors, not positive net rates.

The same cash-flow argument values delivery of n F as a financed foreign deposit costing nS₀/RF H today. This replication needs the actual delivery currency and date. A cash-settled non-deliverable forward (NDF) instead pays a stated H amount using a fixing. For a short position of h F, define its contractual maturity payoff as G=h(K−X), where X is that contract's H/F fixing. If the exporter can convert n F at executable spot S and collect/pay G fully, then:

nS + h(K−X) = hK + (n−h)S + h(S−X).

The identity exposes three amounts: the contracted component, residual notional exposure and fixing-versus-execution basis. At h=n and X=S, total receipts are nK. If either equality fails, a price residual remains. A deliverable forward would instead require actual F delivery to its specified account; an onshore F balance may be unavailable for that delivery. Do not substitute its delivery mechanics for the NDF assumed below.

The original-author international capital-market slides give the covered-investment method and distinguish it from expected uncovered returns. The BIS authors' September 2016 basis analysis explains why executable funding, credit, liquidity and balance-sheet costs matter. Here equality is a theorem inside its assumptions, not a claim that actual midpoint quotes must satisfy it. A departure from equality is not an executable arbitrage until each borrowing, delivery, collateral and settlement leg is verified.

3. Worked case 1: a covered price is not a physical forecast

Take S₀=6/5 H/F, RH=53/50 and RF=51/50. The ideal forward is K=106/85≈1.247059 H/F. A firm expects a fixed gross receipt of 120 F and an enforceably matched cost of 40 F at the same onshore collection event; its resulting net receivable is n=80 F. Those gross flows are not counted again in the later lab. At full performance, unrestricted conversion and X=S, selling h=80 F forward makes total maturity receipts 80 K=1696/17≈99.764706 H.

Suppose a physical scenario analysis assigns probabilities 3/4 and 1/4 to S=1 and S=9/5. Then E[S]=6/5 and expected unhedged receipts are 96 H. The hedged receipts exceed that expectation by 64/17≈3.764706 H. Nothing contradicts parity: the unhedged receipt has different statewise payoffs, and this physical distribution is not a risk-neutral pricing rule. The two-state variance of unhedged receipts is 768 H²; the ideal full hedge's variance is zero. Probabilities, payoffs and discounting cannot be mixed by changing a label.

Even full ideal receipts fall short of a 100 H loan by 4/17 H if there is no other cash. Currency matching does not remove a preexisting value shortfall. A hedge may also be imperfect when revenue volume responds to S: if n itself changes, the identity is statewise with that changing n, not with the budgeted volume. Here n is fixed deliberately so later failures can be attributed to timing, access, fixing and counterparty assumptions.

4. A dated exporter: price, location and settlement are separate

Cedar is one legal corporation with a foreign branch and an offshore H account. The onshore F receivable belongs to that same corporation. There is no automatic pooling across account locations. The following are complete synthetic rights for this case, not statements of existing law:

  1. Before the early margin cutoff Cedar owns u=12 H offshore. A cash-equity injection x≥0, if used, arrives before that cutoff and has no repayment or issue cost during this horizon. Cash earns no interest during these short settlement subperiods.
  2. The earlier collateral requirement is m=ah H, where a is a scenario-specific contractual amount per hedged F. Cedar posts only cash it has. Posted collateral remains its segregated asset and returns in full at a later release date after the external debt cutoff. The schedule is an input, not a derived market value of the forward.
  3. By the debt cutoff, either all 80 F of the net receivable has arrived or none has; a delayed receipt arrives at the later release date. Cedar converts the smaller of arrived F and a conversion cap CF. It transfers the smaller of the resulting H and a separate transfer cap TH. Unconverted F and untransferred H remain onshore assets.
  4. The NDF uses the original specified K=106/85, whatever the later restrictions. A positive G pays only ρG offshore at the cutoff, with the unpaid positive amount permanently lost. A negative G remains fully owed. The parameter ρ is the realized payment fraction, not a default probability. Segregation protects already posted collateral under these stipulated terms.
  5. After the foreign transfer arrives, Cedar settles the negative NDF amount first, then pays D=100 H to its offshore lender. There is no cross-account or cross-contract netting and no unmodeled borrowing. Payments use only cash available; unpaid debt or negative NDF settlement remains a liability.
  6. For a diagnostic continuation after a missed margin call, contracts remain outstanding, later receipts still arrive, and no acceleration, termination or extra penalty occurs. The breach is explicitly flagged; a real contract could end this continuation. The later collateral/receipt release does not retroactively satisfy an earlier cutoff.

Convertibility concerns changing currency. Transferability concerns moving a balance to the required location; an H balance held onshore can still be unavailable offshore. The MIGA 2023 presentation, slide 49 distinguishes conversion and outward transfer restrictions from depreciation in its described insurance product. That historical product distinction is useful vocabulary; it does not insure Cedar, certify today's coverage, or supply our numerical caps.

Let A be the F amount that arrives before cutoff. The usable transfer is t=min{S min(A, CF), TH}. Set G⁺=max(G, 0), G⁻=max(−G, 0), and c=ρG⁺. If every obligation is met, the two relevant cumulative offshore balances are:

B₁=u+x−m;
B₂=u+x−m+t+c−G⁻−D.

Exact cash requirement. Under the listed rights, all collateral and payments are met if and only if

x ≥ x*(h) = max{0, m−u, m+D+G⁻−u−t−c}.

Proof. Full posting requires B₁≥0. With posting completed, all transfer and positive derivative receipts arrive before the two later payments. B₂≥0 therefore funds both, in their stated priority; the balance immediately before paying D is B₂+D≥0. These are all earlier offshore deadlines. Conversely, violation of the first inequality prevents full posting; violation of the second makes total required later payments exceed available cash after full posting. Equality is allowed and produces zero cash at a binding cutoff. A nonnegative injection satisfying both is sufficient. Because x neither changes the flows nor creates a repayment in this window, the maximum is exact. A guarantee paid after the cutoff, an unfunded promise or an onshore asset cannot be substituted for x.

When x is insufficient, this formula is a feasibility certificate, not permission to record negative cash. The lab posts min(available cash, requirement) at each step. It retains unpaid financial liabilities and records unposted collateral separately: an unmet collateral requirement is a breach, not an additional cash loan to the firm. After all receivables and posted collateral are released, translated net assets satisfy the conservation identity:

offshore H + onshore H + S(onshore F) − unpaid NDF − unpaid debt
= u+x+nS+ρG⁺−G⁻−D.

This is a scenario accounting translation with supplied S, without liquidation discounts or discounting between subperiods. It is not a statement of realizable offshore wealth at the earlier cutoff. A negative right side is an economic loss under that convention; a positive right side does not imply timely payment.

5. Worked case 2: the same hedge, several different failures

Keep h=n=80 F. In the weak-currency state S=X=4/5, a=1/20, CF=80, TH=200 and ρ=1. Post 4 H from 12, convert and transfer 64 H, then receive G=608/17 H. Cash before debt is 1832/17 H, so all 100 H is paid and cutoff cash is 132/17 H. Later the posted 4 returns; final net assets are 200/17 H. The clear state S=X=11/10 instead transfers 88 H and receives 200/17 H from the NDF, yielding the same two closing amounts.

For the transfer lock, all 80 F convert into 64 H, but only 40 H moves offshore; 24 H remains onshore. After posting, available debt cash is 8+40+608/17=1424/17 H, leaving 276/17 H owed. Later assets are 4 H offshore plus 24 H onshore; subtracting the unpaid loan gives 200/17 H. Under the conversion lock, only 50 F convert into 40 H and all of that transfers; the trapped asset is instead 30 F, worth 24 H at the stated S. Equal translated amounts do not make the access constraints identical.

In the joint state, post 6 H and transfer 32 H, retaining 8 H and 30 F onshore. The contract's positive payoff is 472/17 H, but only 236/17 H arrives. Debt cash is 6+32+236/17=882/17 H; unpaid debt is 818/17 H. The fixing mismatch reduces full-performance receipts by 8 H, and the counterparty shortfall costs another 236/17 H. Thus final net assets are 200/17−8−236/17=−172/17 H. The lost positive claim is not counted again as a surviving receivable.

In the margin squeeze, the required early 18 H exceeds 12 H. Under the stated diagnostic continuation only 12 is posted; 6 is unposted. The 120 H foreign conversion arrives later, and the NDF owes 344/17 H. Paying it leaves 1696/17 H for the 100 H loan, which is short by 4/17 H. The correct timely injection is 106/17 H: it must fund full early collateral as well as the later loan. Injecting merely 4/17 leaves most of the early breach unresolved. Posted collateral returns only afterward.

The receipt-delay state collects the positive 608/17 H hedge payoff, but not the 64 H foreign conversion before cutoff. It pays only 744/17 H of the loan, leaving 956/17 H due. The late foreign asset still contributes to final translated value. Across these states, the common value 200/17 is therefore compatible with very different earlier outcomes.

6. Choose a hedge for a stated objective

An 80 F hedge eliminates ideal terminal spot exposure. Minimizing the extra cash required before two specified stress cutoffs is a different problem. Keep the weak-currency and margin-squeeze states only, choose a short notional 0≤h≤80 F at the same K, and let collateral scale as ah. The required common early injection is the maximum of five affine functions:

x(h)=max{0, h/20−12, 24−27 h/68, 9 h/40−12, 65 h/136−32} H.

The weak-currency late constraint is 24−27 h/68: unhedged debt cash is short by 24, while each hedged F contributes K−4/5 less its collateral requirement. The margin-squeeze early constraint is 9 h/40−12. Its later constraint includes the negative NDF settlement as well as posted collateral. All coefficients have the implied H/F or H units.

Exact optimum and proof. Weight the early squeeze constraint by 30/47 and the late weak-currency constraint by 17/47. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one; the h coefficients cancel, leaving 48/47 H. Every feasible common injection is at least this convex combination. At h=2720/47≈57.872340 F, both chosen constraints equal 48/47≈1.021277 H. The other early constraint is −428/47 H, and the later squeeze constraint is −204/47 H; the zero constraint is also smaller. Thus x*=48/47 and this h attains the lower bound. No grid search or asymptotic claim is needed. With no hedge x(0)=24 H; with a full hedge x(80)=106/17 H. The optimized hedge leaves 1040/47 F of terminal spot exposure.

For a more general finite selected set, each earlier collateral constraint is affine in h. Because h≥0, the sign of h(K−X) is fixed by K−X, so each later constraint is also affine even with a fixed positive-payment fraction. The maximum of finitely many affine functions is continuous on the compact interval [0, n]. Between all their pairwise intersections its active affine pieces cannot switch; the minimum on each interval occurs at an endpoint or throughout a flat segment. Evaluating the interval endpoints and in-range pairwise intersections therefore finds a global minimum. The lab uses precisely this finite construction and chooses the smallest h in a tie. It does not optimize probabilities, changing quantities, nonlinear margin rules or unlisted states. In particular, the transfer, joint and delay states remain outside this two-state design certificate.

7. Sovereign capacity: a two-currency resource budget

A sovereign's ability to tax, adjust spending or issue its own unit does not constitute a specified F receipt. Foreign-currency payment may require usable reserves, fiscal receipts already collected in F, executable purchases of F, or new financing that actually settles. A domestic-currency printing operation would be a new transaction with possible price and exchange-rate effects; it is absent here. Similarly, export earnings of private residents are not automatically treasury resources. A future fiscal primary surplus is not cash at an earlier deadline.

The public-debt accounting methods in the January 2010 IMF technical note by Escolano, already read in Volume 6, motivate distinguishing stock changes, cash and terminal financing assumptions. Our currency/location constraints are additional original assumptions, not a debt-sustainability threshold supplied by that note. The IEO's 2003 retrospective Korea discussion supplies a dated historical example of why usable reserves and short-term funding matter. It neither calibrates our case nor identifies an intervention's causal effect by itself.

In the following synthetic sovereign account, R F of reserves exist, B F are unavailable until a later release, and a floor f F must remain usable. The stipulated fiscal authority can deploy exactly R−B F; no other public account is silently consolidated. It has H cash Y after primary spending and local-currency debt service L. It first pays L as far as Y allows, then may spend remaining H to buy at most C F from a dealer at S H/F. The dealer transfers actual F and receives the corresponding H; conversion does not manufacture foreign currency. Let b=min{C, max(Y−L, 0)/S}. Fiscal export receipts X F and newly contracted borrowing N F have settled before external payments. Essential import payments M F have priority over maturing foreign principal D F, and the floor is preserved.

A = R−B+X+N+b;
imports paid = min{M, max(A−f, 0)};
foreign principal paid p = min{D, max(A−f−M, 0)}.

The last expression is valid because imports have the stated priority. If A−f< M, import arrears occur and p=0. H local service can also be unpaid, separately. These are conditional capacity payments under an attempt-to-pay policy; they do not predict sovereign behavior. Given full local service and fixed purchase b, the smallest extra F receipt before cutoff that funds imports, foreign debt and the floor is z*=max{0, f+M+D−A}. Necessity follows by adding those required F uses; sufficiency follows by paying them in order. A top-up in F cannot, under this one-way conversion policy, cure a separate earlier H service shortfall. A borrowing top-up also creates a later debt claim; a grant does not.

New N is a financing inflow, not revenue, and it does not erase the old D. If other unmatured foreign principal is O, then closing principal is B₁=D+O+N−p, with any unpaid D still included. Let B₀=D+O and opening exchange rate S₀. With no accrued interest during this snapshot, the H debt-value bridge is:

S B₁−S₀B₀ = (S−S₀)B₀ + S(N−p).

Proof. Substitute B₁=B₀+N−p and distribute S. The first term revalues existing F principal; the second translates the actual new borrowing less repayment at their stipulated transaction rate S. The identity does not turn either revaluation into cash. If interest accrues, debt is forgiven, or several transaction exchange rates apply, record those additional terms at their own times. No constant debt ratio or repeated rollover is a proof that future debt service is feasible.

8. Worked case 3: the same closing debt, different financing histories

The sovereign owns 30 F in reserves, of which 8 F cannot be released until after the cutoff; the usable reserve floor is 4 F. It has 100 H after primary spending, local service of 36 H, foreign principal due of 40 F and other foreign principal of 60 F. These foreign debts are nonresident claims; the local service classification is independent of currency. Any new F loan is principal now and is due later at gross factor 11/10. Blocked reserve release does not change total reserve ownership.

Reference F conservation is 22+10+20+12−12−40=12 usable reserves left. The 8 F blocked account is separate throughout. In the rollover stop, conservation is 22+8+0+6−12−20=4. The missing 20 F is not supplied by the 46 H remaining: the purchase cap already binds at 6 F. Releasing the 8 blocked F only later cannot pay this cutoff; even if it were released before and the floor unchanged, 12 F of the current gap would remain. A timely 20 F grant closes the F gap under fixed behavior. A timely 20 F loan also closes it but adds 20 F principal and its separately contracted future service.

Each case ends with 80 F principal, but the first two consist of 60 F old future principal plus 20 F newly borrowed. The stop consists of 60 F future principal plus 20 F arrears. Equal aggregates hide different maturity and enforcement problems. Opening foreign principal was 100 F at S₀=2, worth 200 H. With depreciation, closing principal is worth 240 H. The +40 H change is +100 H revaluation of old principal and −60 H of net principal transactions. In the reference state it is instead −40 H, with zero revaluation. None of those reporting-value changes pays an extra F.

9. Capacity, willingness and restructuring terms

Capacity asks whether specified resources and rights can satisfy specified obligations. Willingness asks which feasible action an authorized decision-maker chooses, given its objectives and consequences. That second question needs a model of costs, constituencies, strategic responses and enforcement; it is not answered by a cash ratio. A sovereign default may redistribute losses across foreign creditors, resident savers, banks, taxpayers and service recipients. The examples below do not estimate those effects or endorse default.

Worked case 4: an explicit choice and a dated concession

In a separate two-action illustration, assume the sovereign has capacity to pay 50 F, owes 40 F, and compares scores measured in H-equivalent welfare units. Paying fully yields UR=200−40 S. The default/restructuring alternative yields UD=200−90=110, where 90 is an exogenous aggregate consequence in the same units. Full repayment is available only if capacity≥40. Choose repayment on an exact feasible tie. These scores are stipulated preferences, not accounting income or evidence about actual governments; they omit bargaining, partial settlement, dynamic reputation and endogenous future financing.

At S=2, repayment is feasible and its score 120 exceeds 110. At S=3 it remains feasible but its score 80 is lower, so the toy decision selects the default/restructuring alternative. The exact feasible indifference rate is S=9/4. More generally repayment is chosen precisely when capacity≥D and SD≤C, where C is the assumed default consequence. If capacity falls to 39 F, the full-payment action is unavailable even with C=200 H. The capacity ledger of Worked case 3 is a separate conditional attempt-to-pay calculation, not an execution of this preference model.

Now consider one creditor's consent to a maturity extension, separately from those scores. A promised 40 F payment at date 1 is replaced by 44 F at date 2. With supplied positive F discount factors d₁=19/20 and d₂=9/10, original PV is 38 F and replacement PV is 198/5=39.6 F: the creditor PV rises by 8/5 F despite 40 F of date-1 cash relief to the debtor. Equal or larger face principal does not fix the PV effect of a restructuring. Under these factors, the date-2 payment that exactly preserves PV is 380/9 F. These are comparisons using one stated valuation curve, not market prices of uncertain recovery.

Do not assume all creditors can be bound by a favorable aggregate calculation. Participation, amendment thresholds, aggregation across instruments, ranking, guarantees, immunity and enforcement must be verified for the actual instrument and forum. A court judgment, insurance entitlement or policy announcement may create a claim without making the required currency available by tomorrow. An insurance payout requires its own covered event, documentation, waiting period, exclusions and settlement date. Those are additional inputs, not hidden rows of the present ledger.

10. From a country label to a decision file

Country risk is a bundle of exposures, not a common haircut that can be applied twice to every instrument. A sovereign stress can reduce bank funding, change the exchange rate, impair a hedge counterparty and restrict transfers together. Build one joint state, revalue each owned claim once, then follow actual payments. Adding the worst currency loss from one state to the worst default loss from an incompatible state needs a new scenario justification. Conversely, a currency hedge does not eliminate local borrower credit, sovereign fiscal exposure, a nonresident funding run or legal uncertainty.

Capital-flow analysis must distinguish new borrowing, repayment, rollover negotiations, portfolio revaluation and the availability of proceeds. In the sovereign example, N=20 F is a new loan received before the old 40 F comes due; N=0 is a contractual financing stop, not automatically a change in exports. At a national level gross flows may be large despite a small net flow. The accepted external-account identities reconcile those flows; they do not supply a behavioral reason creditors will renew. A country current-account improvement can coexist with an earlier cash squeeze.

A useful decision file therefore contains the claim map, governing documents and unresolved legal questions; the currency/account cash ladder; a joint state and the assumptions linking it to exposures; alternative funded actions with dates; and the residuals that each action leaves. A hedge can be judged on terminal exposure, expected utility, accounting volatility or cash feasibility, but the objective must be stated. Reducing one residual may increase another. An extension beyond this chapter would estimate joint cash-flow and access dynamics, endogenize sovereign and creditor decisions, and validate legal and operational assumptions with qualified practitioners. No single synthetic stress certifies those tasks.

Reproduce the claim and cash ledgers

The portable lab includes synthetic inputs, standard-library implementation, exact saved output, four-payload integrity manifest and contract and execution guide. It returns exact rational strings, seven exporter states, the finite hedge-design certificate, three sovereign capacity ledgers, the separate two-action choice and the dated PV comparison. The model distinguishes actual funded partial payments from full-payment feasibility. Change a restriction, timing flag, realized payment fraction or funding source one at a time, then explain which cash account changes. The independent checker also validates manuscript fractions rather than treating a saved-output match as proof of prose accuracy.

Exercises

  1. Covered trades and quotation. Use S₀=6/5, RH=53/50 and RF=51/50. Prove the forward equality under explicit executable-trade assumptions. At K=13/10 construct the funded trade starting with 120 H borrowed; at K=6/5 construct the reverse trade starting with 100 F borrowed. Show both maturity profits in H. If S rises from 6/5 to 3/2, calculate the percentage change in H/F and in the reciprocal F/H quote. Explain why actual asymmetric borrowing terms could invalidate the trades.
  2. Exposure and probability. Solve Worked case 1's two-state physical distribution from the prompt values S=1, 9/5 with probabilities 3/4, 1/4, n=80, K=106/85. Find expected unhedged receipts, their variance, full-hedge receipts and the difference between expected hedged and unhedged receipts. Derive nS+h(K−X). State exactly which equalities give a constant nK and why parity alone cannot supply the physical probabilities or E[S].
  3. A transfer is not a translation. In the transfer-lock state, calculate every offshore cash step, onshore balances, unpaid debt and later translated net assets. Repeat the asset-location conclusion for conversion cap 50 F with transfer cap 200 H. Prove the general x*(h) formula including its sufficiency assumptions. Find the smallest early H cash-equity contribution for either state. Explain why the 4 H collateral release alone does not fix the original cutoff.
  4. Basis, credit and maturity. Recompute the joint state, separating the 8 H fixing loss and counterparty loss from the liquidity restriction. Show the final-value conservation identity and all surviving liabilities. Then compute the receipt-delay state's debt arrears and early cash requirement, with other weak-currency inputs unchanged. Explain why a deliverable forward of 80 F would require a different access test, and why a recovery probability cannot be inserted as if it were a realized same-day payment fraction.
  5. Prove the limited hedge-design optimum. Use only weak-currency and margin-squeeze states, 0≤h≤80, and the five affine constraints in Section 6. Derive the two binding constraints from cash flows, establish a lower bound valid for every h, find h and x attaining it, and check the three other constraints. Compute the remaining unhedged F amount. Compare h=0 and h=80. Does this certificate cover transfer locks or minimize all definitions of risk? State the precise finite-candidate argument used by the lab.
  6. Sovereign currencies and rollover. Reconstruct the reference and rollover-stop ledgers in Worked case 3, including the dealer's H receipt, the remaining H cash, blocked and usable F, and the composition of closing foreign principal. Derive and check the H debt-value bridge using S₀=2. In the stop, find the effect of (a) releasing the 8 blocked F before cutoff, (b) a 20 F grant before cutoff, and (c) a 20 F new loan due later at 11/10. Keep all other policy terms fixed. Which changes pay the original cutoff, and what remains owed later?
  7. Capacity, willingness and valuation. Derive the full feasible-repayment condition in the two-action model. Give its decisions at S=2, S=3 and S=9/4; then reduce F capacity to 39 with C=200. Independently compare the 40 F date-1 promise to 44 F at date 2 using 19/20 and 9/10 discount factors, and find the date-2 amount preserving PV. A memo calls maturity extension both “debt forgiveness” and “guaranteed solvency restoration.” Assess both claims within the actual information given.
  8. Cross-border decision critique. A board memo says: “The group owns enough translated assets, all foreign-currency debt is external debt, foreign-law bonds always recover in full, a full forward hedge removes country risk, and 20 F of reserves released next week covers today's 20 F gap.” Write a replacement recommendation. Correct each claim, propose three independently executable verification steps, distinguish what the lab proves from what needs new legal or empirical evidence, and specify one funded contingency with a date and residual risk. Use an explicit assessment rubric rather than claiming one universally correct policy.
Complete solutions

  1. Borrowing S₀ H, depositing 1 F and forward-selling RF gives KRF−S₀RH. The reverse financed position gives its negative. Both require common maturity and credit, executable two-way funding/spot/forward, no costs, restrictions or unmodeled collateral; no-arbitrage therefore gives 106/85 H/F. At 13/10, 120 H buys 100 F; the foreign deposit pays 102 F, forward proceeds are 663/5 H and domestic repayment 636/5 H, leaving 27/5 H. At 6/5, borrow 100 F, sell for 120 H, invest to 636/5 H, and buy 102 F for 612/5 H to repay; profit 24/5 H. Every foreign liability is covered. Different borrowing and lending rates or inaccessible accounts change actual legs and may erase either apparent profit.

    The H/F rise is(3/2)/(6/5)−1=1/4=25%. The reciprocal quote falls from 5/6 to 2/3 F/H; its change is(2/3)/(5/6)−1=−1/5=−20%. Finite percentage changes do not simply negate under inversion.

  2. E[S]=(3/4)1+(1/4)(9/5)=6/5. Receipt values are 80 H and 144 H, so the mean is 96 H and variance(3/4)(80−96)²+(1/4)(144−96)²=768 H². Full ideal receipts are 1696/17 H; their difference from 96 is 64/17 H, with variance zero under the stated two-state payoffs. Algebra gives nS+hK−hX=hK+(n−h)S+h(S−X). Fixed n=h and X=S in every state make it nK. A changing n, fixing mismatch, payment failure or access restriction breaks a different premise. Covered trades contain no physical expectation; a mean greater or less than K is not by itself a covered arbitrage or a pricing probability.

  3. Post 4 from 12, leaving 8 H. Convert 80 F into 64 H; transfer 40, leaving 24 H onshore and 48 H offshore before the NDF. Receive 608/17 H to reach 1424/17 H; all goes to the 100 H lender, leaving 276/17 H owed and zero cutoff cash. Later 4 H returns, giving 4+24−276/17=200/17 H net assets. For the conversion lock, convert 50 F into 40 H and transfer all 40; the onshore balance is 30 F instead of 24 H, with the same translated value 24 H and the same offshore trail.

    With full posting, the necessary balances are u+x−m and u+x−m+t+ρG⁺−G⁻−D. Taking their nonnegative requirements and x≥0 gives the stated maximum. When transfers/positive receipts precede both later payments, these inequalities also fund every intermediate payment; no later deadline is used to fund an earlier one. Thus x*=276/17 H for each lock. At exactly that injection, the loan is fully paid with zero cutoff cash and 4 H remains posted. Without the injection, a later 4 H return could reduce arrears only afterward, still leaving 208/17 H unpaid if applied then; it cannot rewrite the original missed cutoff. No automatic late debt repayment is included in the lab's saved trail.

  4. Joint collateral is 6 H, leaving 6. Convert 50 F into 40 H, transfer 32 and retain 8 H plus 30 F onshore. G=80(106/85−9/10)=472/17 H; atρ=1/2 collect 236/17 H and write off the other 236/17. Available debt cash is 882/17 H, all paid, leaving 818/17 H owed. Later cash includes returned 6 H, so 6+8+(4/5)30−818/17=−172/17 H. There is no negative-NDF liability in this state and no surviving claim for the written-off positive amount. The direct identity is 12+64+236/17−100=−172/17. Relative to ideal full matching, 80(S−X)=−8 H and counterparty loss 236/17 H explain the value difference; transfer/segregation changes timing and location separately.

    For receipt delay, post 4; no F has arrived and no H transfers. Cash for debt is 8+608/17=744/17 H, leaving 956/17 H due. Full timely injection is 956/17 H; after the original cutoff the 80 F receipt and 4 H collateral release explain later net value 200/17 H but not timely payment. A deliverable contract requires 80 F at its delivery account, so blocked or late F must be tested against that obligation. A probability describes uncertain outcomes;ρ here is the actual fraction paid by a specified cutoff. Taking an expectation cannot manufacture the realized cash in a bad state.

  5. In the weak state, usable foreign conversion is 64 H and each short hedged F produces 106/85−4/5=38/85 H but locks 1/20 H early; the late injection constraint is 100−12−64+h(1/20−38/85)=24−27 h/68. Early high-margin posting needs 9 h/40−12. Their 30/47 and 17/47 weighted average is 48/47 for every h, proving a lower bound. Equate them: h(9/40+27/68)=36, giving h=2720/47 F and x=48/47 H. At this h, weak early requirement is−428/47 H, squeeze late is−204/47 H, and 0 is smaller than 48/47. The lower bound is attained. Residual exposure is 80−2720/47=1040/47 F.

    At h=0 the maximum is 24 H. At h=80 the early squeeze needs 6 H and its late constraint 106/17 H dominates, while weak late is−132/17 H; thus x=106/17 H. The optimum only minimizes common early equity-funded cash across two fixed states. It does not cover the other five states, expected utility or terminal FX variance. For finitely many affine constraints, subdivide[0, n] at their pairwise intersections. On each piece no ordering changes, so an active affine line governs the maximum; a minimum lies at an endpoint or a flat segment's endpoints. The finite candidate list therefore includes a minimizer, including interval boundaries and degeneracies.

  6. Local service pays 36 H first. Reference buys 12 F for 24 H, leaving 40 H. Usable F before external payments is 22+10+20+12=64. Pay imports 12 and debt 40, leaving 12 usableF and 8 blockedF. Closing foreign principal is 40+60+20−40=80 F, consisting of 60 old future and 20 new; the new loan later requires 22 F. In the stop, buy 6 F for 18 H, leaving 46 H. F resources are 22+8+0+6=36; after 12 imports and 20 debt, 4 usableF remains. There are 20 F arrears and 60 F future principal, again 80 total. The cap prevents spending the remaining 46 H to obtain more F.

    Substitution gives S(B₀+N−p)−S₀B₀=(S−S₀)B₀+S(N−p). Reference change is 0+2(20−40)=−40 H. Stop change is(3−2)100+3(0−20)=100−60=40 H, exactly 3(80)−2(100). Depreciation-only produces the same +40 H bridge withN 20, p 40, but no arrears.

    Releasing 8 F early raises payment from 20 to 28 and leaves 12 F owed; it changes access, not total assets. A 20 F grant before cutoff pays all 40 and leaves the 4 F floor; remaining foreign principal is 60 F and no new loan service arises. A 20 F loan before cutoff also pays all 40 but leaves 60+20=80 F principal and adds 22 F later service. The grant and loan close today's gap; neither proves payment of every future obligation. The blocked 8 F's original later release remains separate unless intervention(a) explicitly moves its date.

  7. Full payment is feasible iff capacity≥D. When feasible, UR≥UD iffY−SD≥Y−C, equivalentlySD≤C. At S 2, 120> 110: repay. At S 3, 80< 110: choose the modeled default/restructuring alternative. At S 9/4 both scores 110, so the tie rule repays. With capacity 39< 40, full payment is unavailable even with default cost 200; the formula for its hypothetical score does not make it feasible.

    The original PV is 40(19/20)=38 F; the replacement is 44(9/10)=198/5 F, a gain 8/5 F. Preserving PV requires amount 38/(9/10)=380/9 F at date 2. Cash relief at date 1 is 40 F, but neither a smaller discounted creditor claim nor forgiveness follows from the extension label. The debtor now owes 44 F later; future receipts, financing, other claims and participation conditions are unspecified. Solvency restoration therefore cannot be certified. Different discount assumptions or uncertain payment would require a new valuation.

  8. A defensible recommendation conditions the decision on the actual entity, currencies, accounts and dates. Translated assets can be blocked, late or costly to sell. External debt classification depends on creditor residence, not denomination. A foreign-law label requires contract/forum/enforcement analysis and cannot imply full recovery. The hedge identity controls only specified amount/fixing/performance assumptions; country credit, transfer, counterparty and earlier margin risks remain. Next week's reserves cannot settle today's obligation without an additional bridge whose lender, currency, amount and repayment are identified.

    Three concrete checks are: reconcile account-level usable balances and release notices to the exact cutoff; independently confirm derivative/collateral settlement, fixing and enforceable netting rights with the counterparty and appropriate legal review; and test committed funding, currency purchase capacity and later repayment against one joint scenario. Each check needs dated evidence, a responsible owner and a consequence if it fails. One conditional contingency is a 20 F irrevocable funded contribution received before the sovereign cutoff; it removes the modeled F shortfall but requires an identified provider and does not solve later debt or willingness. A 20 F loan is a different contingency because it creates future service.

    Rubric, 12 points. Award 1 for each of the five corrected claims; 1 for each of three executable checks with its evidence; 2 for a fully dated and funded contingency and its residual; 1 for separating the exact finite-model certificate from legal/empirical questions; 1 for an accountable conditional recommendation rather than a guaranteed outcome. An answer using later or trapped cash as if presently usable, or counting the same loss twice, must repair that critical error before receiving a mastery pass. Alternatives earn full credit when their rights, resources, dates and limits are equally explicit.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In three minutes, explain to a credit committee how Cedar can have a full currency hedge, positive later translated net assets and an unpaid loan. Use the transfer-lock state rather than a metaphor. Answer standard: state K and the assumptions behind 1696/17 H ideal receipts; show 4 H collateral is unavailable, only 40 H transfers and 608/17 H settles from the NDF; identify 276/17 H arrears and 24 H remaining onshore; then reconcile 4+24−276/17=200/17 H later net assets. A strong explanation proposes a timed remedy without treating the return of collateral as an earlier receipt.

Delayed check, seven days later. Without the solutions, answer: (1)Does external mean foreign currency? (2)What is the physical FX mean implied by CIP? (3)What are Cedar's two full-payment prefix inequalities? (4)Why is the optimum 2720/47 F not a universal hedge recommendation? (5)What does new 20 F borrowing do to the sovereign's old 40 F payment? (6)Can a maturity extension improve liquidity while raising creditor PV?

Answers and remediation

(1)No: use creditor residence for the external-account classification, and map denomination separately; revisit Section 1. (2)None is implied: parity is a covered-price restriction under executable trades, not a physical expectation; reconstruct Section 2's two loans. (3)u+x−m≥0 andu+x−m+t+ρG⁺−G⁻−D≥0; locate every receipt before using it. (4)It minimizes a common early cash injection for only two specified affine states while leaving 1040/47 F residual exposure; redo the weighted lower bound. (5)It supplies a new receipt with a later liability; old 40 F remains due and must actually be paid. ReconcileN andp separately. (6)Yes: 40 at date 1 becomes 44 at date 2, removing 40 of early cash need while PV rises from 38 to 198/5 under the given curve. Recompute the cash dates before discussing solvency. For an oral extension, replace the cash injection by a loan repayable before the foreign receivable: the original minimum formula no longer applies without another prefix and a financed repayment.

Sources and further study

  • International Monetary Fund — Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, Seventh Edition: March 2025 White Cover (Pre-Edited) Version — Resident external accounts, financial-account signs, statistical discrepancy, saving-current-account bridge, integrated IIP, valuation and residence reclassification; BPM7 terminology mapped to older BPM6 labels.
  • Stephanie Schmitt-Grohé, Martín Uribe and Michael Woodford — International Macroeconomics: A Modern Approach, Chapter 11 author slides: International Capital Market Integration (6 September 2022) — Covered investment and arbitrage paths, conditional expected uncovered returns and why free capital mobility alone does not imply UIP.
  • Claudio Borio, Robert McCauley, Patrick McGuire and Vladyslav Sushko — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016) — Primary author discussion of executable covered positions, FX hedging, bid/ask and funding frictions, counterparty/liquidity risks and costly balance sheets.
  • MIGA — Political Risk Insurance and Credit Enhancement Solutions, 2023 Annual Meetings presentation — Historical product-specific distinction between currency conversion restrictions, outward transfer restrictions and depreciation. It does not supply current national law, actual coverage for the synthetic firm or the numerical restrictions in the chapter.
  • Julio Escolano — A Practical Guide to Public Debt Dynamics, Fiscal Sustainability, and Cyclical Adjustment of Budgetary Aggregates (IMF Technical Notes and Manuals 10/02, January 2010) — Exact debt/GDP accounting and the distinction between constant ratios, stability and explicit terminal financing restrictions; no historical estimates imported.
  • IMF Independent Evaluation Office (2003), The IMF and Recent Capital Account Crises: Indonesia, Korea, Brazil — Chapter 2 — Dated retrospective Korea 1997 chronology: short-term foreign bank funding, usable versus headline reserves, 4 December program and continued funding pressure. Synthetic numerical examples are not sourced country estimates.
